questions.question_text: Under Virginia's Condominium Act, how many days does a buyer have to cancel a new unit purchase from a developer?
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-1974 gives a purchaser buying a new condominium unit from the declarant the right to cancel within five calendar days after the contract date or after delivery of the current public offering statement, whichever is later.

questions.question_text: A buyer receives the resale certificate for a Virginia condominium and the contract sets no review period. How long is the cancellation period?
questions.explanation: Since July 1, 2025 condominium and POA resales both run through the Virginia Resale Disclosure Act. Va. Code § 55.1-2312 lets the parties set the review period in the contract; absent one, the purchaser has three days from receipt of the resale certificate (or notice that it is unavailable) to cancel. That is separate from the five-day right in § 55.1-1974 for new units bought from the declarant.

questions.question_text: Where must a Virginia condominium developer register before offering units for sale?
questions.correct_answer: Common Interest Community Board within DPOR
distractors: Department of Housing and Urban Development
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-1976 requires the declarant to register the condominium with the Common Interest Community Board, which sits within DPOR, before offering units for sale.

questions.question_text: A condo owner fails to pay assessments. How does the association's lien priority compare to a first deed of trust?
questions.correct_answer: The lien is subordinate to the first deed of trust
distractors: The lien takes priority over all other liens
The lien is equal to the first deed of trust
No lien attaches for unpaid assessments
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-1966 gives a condominium unit owners' association a lien for unpaid assessments that is prior to other liens except real estate tax liens and the lien of a first mortgage or first deed of trust recorded before the assessment came due. Virginia has no 'super-lien' priority over the first lender.

questions.question_text: What document must a developer provide to a Virginia condo buyer before sale?
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-1973 requires the declarant to deliver a current public offering statement, which discloses the condominium instruments, budget, warranties, and the purchaser's cancellation rights.

questions.question_text: Under VRLTA, what is the maximum security deposit a Virginia landlord may collect?
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-1226 forbids a landlord to demand or receive a security deposit, however denominated, exceeding two months' periodic rent. (When a licensee holds the funds, 18VAC135-20-181 and Va. Code § 54.1-2108.1 govern the escrow account.)

questions.question_text: A Virginia tenant moves out. Within how many days must the landlord return the security deposit?
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-1226 requires the landlord to give the tenant written, itemized notice of deductions, damages, and charges together with any balance due within 45 days after the termination date of the tenancy or the date the tenant vacates, whichever occurs last.

questions.question_text: A Virginia tenant subject to the VRLTA fails to pay rent. What notice must the landlord serve before terminating the tenancy for nonpayment?
questions.explanation: SB 48/HB 15 (2026), effective July 1, 2026, lengthened the nonpayment notice in Va. Code § 55.1-1245 F from five days to 14 days. For other material breaches, § 55.1-1245 A still requires a notice stating the tenancy ends no less than 30 days after receipt if the breach is not remedied within 21 days. Landlords owning four or more units must also offer a payment plan when the arrearage is one month's rent or less.

questions.question_text: A Virginia landlord changes the locks while a tenant is at work to force them out. Is this lawful?
distractors: Yes, if rent is 30 days overdue
Only if the lease specifically allows it
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-1243.1 prohibits self-help eviction — lockouts, utility shutoffs, and removing a tenant's belongings. The landlord must obtain possession through an unlawful detainer action in general district court.

questions.question_text: Under HB 2430, effective July 1, 2025, where must a Virginia landlord itemize the tenant's charges in a written lease?
questions.correct_answer: On the first page of the lease
distractors: On the last page before signatures
In the lease table of contents
questions.explanation: HB 2430, effective for rental agreements entered into, extended, or renewed on or after July 1, 2025, requires the first page of the lease to itemize the security deposit, the rent due per payment period, and any one-time charges due before the commencement date or included in the first rent payment, immediately below a statement that no additional security deposits or rent may be charged unless listed there or added by a later addendum.

questions.question_text: A buyer purchasing a home in a Virginia property owners' association receives the resale certificate, and the contract sets no review period. How long does the buyer have to cancel?
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-2312, part of the Virginia Resale Disclosure Act that took effect July 1, 2025, gives the purchaser the review period agreed in the contract or, if none is stated, three days from receipt of the resale certificate or from notice that it is unavailable. The Act replaced the old POA 'association disclosure packet' and the separate condominium resale certificate with one document.

questions.question_text: A seller's agent requests the resale certificate from a property owners' association. How long does the association have to deliver it?
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-2309 gives the association, its managing agent, or the third-party preparer 14 days from the written request to deliver the resale certificate. If it is not delivered in that window it is deemed unavailable, and the Common Interest Community Board may assess a monetary penalty against the association or manager.

questions.question_text: A homeowner in a Virginia planned community stops paying assessments. What remedy does the POA have?
questions.correct_answer: File a lien and potentially foreclose
distractors: Suspend the owner's voting rights only
Report the debt to credit agencies only
Revoke the owner's deed to the property
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-1833 gives a property owners' association a lien on the lot for unpaid assessments, perfected by memorandum filed in the circuit court clerk's office, and § 55.1-1834 permits enforcement by suit to foreclose the lien.

questions.question_text: What information must a Virginia resale certificate contain for a property owners' association?
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-2310 requires the resale certificate to disclose current assessments and fees, the association's financial statements and reserve information, pending litigation, governing documents and rules, insurance information (including responsibility for a master policy deductible), and restrictions on matters such as flags, solar devices, signs, parking, home businesses, and rentals.

questions.question_text: May a Virginia association charge for preparing a resale certificate, and how is the amount limited?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, up to maximum fees set by the Common Interest Community Board
distractors: Yes, any amount the association considers reasonable
No, it must be provided at no cost
Only for communities with 50 or more lots
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-2316 authorizes fees for preparing, updating, expediting, and delivering the resale certificate but caps them at the maximums established by the Common Interest Community Board, which must be adjusted for inflation using the CPI-U at least every five years. Delivery is still due within 14 days of the request under § 55.1-2309.

questions.question_text: Before excavating in Virginia, who must a contractor contact?
questions.explanation: Virginia's Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act (Va. Code § 56-265.14 et seq.) requires an excavator to submit a locate request to the notification center, VA811 (Miss Utility), before excavating. Operators then mark their underground lines and post a positive response.

questions.question_text: Under Virginia's Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, when may an excavator begin digging after submitting a locate request?
questions.correct_answer: After 48 hours running from 7:00 a.m. the next working day
distractors: After 24 hours from the time of the request
After seven calendar days from the request
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 56-265.17 requires the excavator to wait 48 hours, measured from 7:00 a.m. on the next working day after the locate request is submitted, and to confirm through the notification center's positive response system that operators have marked their lines. The waiting period does not apply to a statutory emergency.

questions.question_text: A homeowner digs a fence post hole without calling 811 and hits a gas line. What consequences apply?
questions.correct_answer: Fines and liability for the damage
distractors: Only a verbal warning for first offense
The utility company absorbs all costs
questions.explanation: The Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act applies to residential excavation, and the State Corporation Commission may impose civil penalties for failing to submit a locate request. The excavator is also liable for damage to the utility's facilities.

questions.question_text: After a contractor calls 811, what must utility companies do?
questions.correct_answer: Mark underground utility locations on site
distractors: Send a representative to supervise digging
Provide blueprints of all utility lines
questions.explanation: Under Va. Code § 56-265.19 operators must mark the approximate horizontal location of their underground facilities with color-coded paint, flags, or stakes and post a response in the notification center's positive response system before the excavation may begin.

questions.question_text: Does Virginia's call-before-you-dig law apply to a homeowner planting a tree in their own yard?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, it applies to all excavation
distractors: Only if digging deeper than 24 inches
Only within 10 feet of the street
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 56-265.15 defines excavation broadly — any operation moving or displacing earth by any tools or equipment, expressly including hand digging with shovels and manual post hole diggers. The only carve-out is installing a metal, plastic, or wooden sign pole placed by hand or foot without tools, so homeowners planting trees or setting fence posts must submit a locate request.
